# A Strategic Coordination Framework of Small LLMs Matches Large LLMs in Data Synthesis

Xin Gao Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory
Email: [gaoxin@pjlab.org.cn](mailto:)    Qizhi Pei Affiliation: Renmin
University of China Email: [wulijun@pjlab.org.cn](mailto:)    Zinan Tang
Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory

AI Laboratory    Honglin Lin Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory

###### Abstract

While data synthesis and distillation are promising strategies to
enhance small language models, current approaches heavily rely on Large
Language Models (LLMs), which suffer from high computational costs,
environmental inefficiency, and potential biases inherited from
monolithic architectures. In contrast, smaller LLMs are more accessible
and sustainable, but their individual capabilities often fall short in
generating high-quality, diverse, and reliable data. Inspired by
collaborative human processes (e.g., peer review), we propose a multiple
small LLMs involved framework, GRA, that aggregates specialized roles
across small LLMs to iterative refinement and quality control typically
achieved by a single large LLM. In this collaborative framework,
multiple small LLMs assume distinct roles—Generator, Reviewer, and
Adjudicator—to simulate a peer-review-inspired data synthesis pipeline.
The Generator proposes initial data samples, the Reviewer critiques
their quality and diversity, and the Adjudicator resolves conflicts to
finalize the output. By decomposing the synthesis process into
specialized sub-tasks, collaborative small LLMs can achieve data-level
parity with large LLM-based distillation. Through experiments across
multiple benchmarks, we demonstrate that GRA-produced data matches or
exceeds the quality of single large LLM outputs, e.g.,
Qwen-2.5-72B-Instruct. Our results challenge the necessity of monolithic
large models for high-quality data synthesis, advocating instead for
strategic coordination of smaller agents. Our datasets, models, and code
are publicly available at
[https://github.com/GX-XinGao/GRA](https://github.com/GX-XinGao/GRA).

Figure 1: Average performance across GRA, vanilla seed dataset and

## 1 Introduction

The advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) with hundreds of billions of
parameters has revolutionized artificial intelligence [Dubey et al.
(2024a)](#bib.bib11); [Yang et al. (2024a)](#bib.bib44); [OpenAI et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib32); [Liu et al. (2024)](#bib.bib26), achieving
state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance across diverse domains such as
natural language understanding [Naveed et al. (2023)](#bib.bib30),
reasoning [Guo et al. (2025)](#bib.bib14); [OpenAI (2024)](#bib.bib31),
math problem solving [Ahn et al. (2024)](#bib.bib1), and code
generation [Jiang et al. (2024)](#bib.bib20). Despite their remarkable
capabilities, these monolithic models demand immense computational
resources and energy, posing significant barriers to deployment in
resource-constrained scenarios like edge devices or latency-sensitive
applications [Zheng et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib50). This paradox has
spurred growing interest in developing smaller-scale LLMs that balance
efficiency and effectiveness, positioning compact yet capable models as
a critical research frontier in sustainable AI [Chen and Varoquaux
(2024)](#bib.bib5).

To enhance small LLMs performance, knowledge distillation [Hinton
(2015)](#bib.bib18)—transferring capabilities from large models via data
synthesis—has emerged as a dominant paradigm [Xu et al.
(2024b)](#bib.bib42). However, conventional distillation inherently
depends on the availability of powerful LLMs [Wang et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib40), which introduces practical limitations: deploying
large LLMs for data generation incurs prohibitive costs, especially in
privacy-sensitive or security-critical scenarios requiring local
execution [Hagos et al. (2024)](#bib.bib15); [Yao et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib46). While small LLMs offer computational accessibility,
their individual capacities are inherently constrained, struggling to
match the quality, diversity, and reliability of data synthesized by
their larger counterparts. This raises a pivotal question: Can we design
a resource-efficient framework that enables small models to collectively
rival the distillation capabilities of monolithic LLMs?

To address this challenge, we propose GRA, a collaborative framework
inspired by human peer-review mechanisms. Diverging from traditional
single-model distillation, GRA orchestrates multiple specialized small
LLMs into three synergistic roles: (1) Generator, which proposes
candidate data samples; (2) Reviewer, which evaluates quality and
diversity through iterative critiques; and (3) Adjudicator, which
resolves conflicts to finalize outputs. Notably, the synthetic data
generated by a single Generator will be evaluated by multiple Reviewers,
and the Adjudicator is to resolve significant disagreements among the
Reviewers by reassessing the data. By decomposing the synthesis pipeline
into discrete sub-tasks and enabling role-specific optimization, GRA
mimics the refinement processes typically concentrated within a single
large LLM. This collaborative architecture not only circumvents the
resource-intensity of large models but also amplifies small models’
collective intelligence through task specialization and iterative
quality control—effectively operationalizing the “wisdom of crowds”
principle in model ensembles.

We validate GRA through extensive experiments on multiple domains,
including general question answering, reasoning, mathematical and coding
tasks. Remarkably, our framework achieves data quality comparable to or
exceeding outputs from SOTA monolithic LLMs like Qwen-2.5-72B-Instruct,
while requiring orders-of-magnitude fewer computational resources. These
results empirically demonstrate that strategically coordinated small
LLMs can collectively surpass the distillation performance of individual
large LLMs.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Data Synthesis

The rapid evolution of LLMs has increased the demand for high-quality,
diverse training data, creating a bottleneck in AI development [Zhao
et al. (2023)](#bib.bib48). Synthetic data is a promising direction to
improve data. A dominant paradigm for synthetic data leverages knowledge
distillation from LLMs. WizardLM [Xu et al. (2024a)](#bib.bib41)
iteratively enhances seed data based on predefined evolutionary rules
and instructions. MAGPIE [Xu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib43) utilizes
pre-defined query templates to directly prompt the LLM to synthesize
data while not relying on seed data. MuggleMath [Li et al.
(2024a)](#bib.bib23) employs LLMs to rewrite and enhance seed datasets
by generating new variations of problem statements and corresponding
answers.

In addition to single-LLM-based approaches, several works also employ
multiple agents for data generation [Mitra et al. (2024)](#bib.bib29);
[Majumdar et al. (2024)](#bib.bib28). AgentInstruct [Mitra et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib29) leverages GPT-4 [OpenAI et al. (2023)](#bib.bib32)
to facilitate data generation and curation through the use of multiple
agents. Similarly, Genetic Instruct [Majumdar et al. (2024)](#bib.bib28)
defines three distinct roles—Instructor-LLM, Coder-LLM, and Judge-LLM—to
generate code data. Unlike previous multi-agent frameworks that rely on
a single LLM like GPT-4 for repeated deployment across different stages,
GRA pioneers a collaborative paradigm that coordinates diverse types of
small LLMs through specialized role allocation to collectively rival the
synthetic data quality of singular large LLMs.

### 2.2 Data Curation

The efficacy of synthetic data critically hinges on post-synthesis
curation [Long et al. (2024)](#bib.bib27). Early curation methodologies
predominantly relied on surface-level heuristics, such as repetition
counts [Salkar et al. (2022)](#bib.bib35) and lexical diversity
metrics [Li et al. (2016)](#bib.bib24); [Zhu et al. (2018)](#bib.bib52);
[Shu et al. (2019)](#bib.bib36), which inadequately captured semantic
coherence and task-specific utility. Recent works shift toward
LLM-driven curation frameworks. Initial efforts employed perplexity
(PPL) and instruction following difficulty score(IFD) [Li et al.
(2024b)](#bib.bib25) to filter low-quality samples. The emergence of
“LLM-as-judge” paradigms further revolutionized this domain, leveraging
well-tuned LLMs for quality assessment [Gu et al. (2024)](#bib.bib13).
In contrast, while sharing the “LLM-as-judge” basis, our GRA framework
differs by using multiple specialized small LLMs for diverse
evaluations. Unlike single-LLM approaches that risk bias, GRA employs a
multi-agent system and a two-tier adjudication to ensure balanced and
comprehensive data assessment.

## 3 Methodology

![Refer to caption](2504.12322v2/overview.png)

Figure 2: Overview of GRA’s architecture, highlighting its four key
modules: (a) The Generator creates domain-specific samples, (b) followed
by collaborative evaluation by Reviewers, (c) The Adjudicator resolves
conflicts, and (d) Post-Processing refines the results by removing
redundancies.

#### Preliminary

We first provide essential background and definitions for key components
with the rationale behind our design choices. Specifically, we denote
$`\mathcal{M}`$ as the pool of small LLMs employed in the framework, and
data pool at iteration $`t`$ as
$`\mathcal{D}^{(t)}=\{(x_{i},y_{i},d_{i},k_{i},s_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}`$,
where each sample in $`\mathcal{D}^{(t)}`$ consists of an instruction
$`x_{i}`$, a response $`y_{i}`$, a domain label $`d_{i}`$, a 3-tuple of
keywords $`k_{i}`$, and a summary $`s_{i}`$. The domain label $`d_{i}`$
indicates the task type of the sample, which is categorized into seven
domains: Coding, Math, Question and Answering, Reasoning, Role Play,
Language, and Creation, which are designed to aim for covering the most
general domains. The 3-tuple keywords $`k_{i}`$ are generated by LLMs to
capture the core concepts of each data sample. In addition, we include a
summary $`s_{i}`$ to provide context and clarify keyword relationships,
enhancing the overall understanding of the data. More details such as
domain definitions and construction of $`\mathcal{D}^{(0)}`$-seed
dataset are shown in the
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Generation ‣ A Strategic Coordination Framework of Small LLMs Matches Large LLMs in Data Synthesis").

### 3.1 Pipeline Overview

The overview of our GRA is shown in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ A Strategic Coordination Framework of Small LLMs Matches Large LLMs in Data Synthesis").
GRA integrates domain-specific generation with collaborative curation by
orchestrating three specialized roles. First, the Generator produces
initial samples using few-shot prompting tailored to the domain. Next,
multiple Reviewers collaboratively assess the quality of these samples.
Finally, an Adjudicator resolves any conflicting evaluations through
consensus-driven arbitration. A post-processing module further refines
the results by eliminating redundant outputs via embedding deduplication
and metadata enrichment. Moreover, to prevent model specialization bias,
GRA dynamically assigns distinct LLMs from $`\mathcal{M}`$ to each role
through random selection and during generation.

### 3.2 Data Generator

To enhance synthetic data diversity while maintaining domain
consistency, we carefully design the generation process to
systematically integrate conceptual knowledge and contextual patterns.
For each instance, we randomly select one LLM $`M_{G}\in\mathcal{M}`$ as
the Generator. For a given domain, the generation workflow comprises
three coordinated stages: First, $`M_{G}`$ analyzes randomly selected
keywords-summary pairs ($`k_{i},s_{i}`$) from the current domain corpus,
synthesizing a novel 3-tuple keywords $`k^{\prime}`$ by extracting and
combining meaningful semantic patterns and attributes from the input
data. Second, drawing inspiration from contextual summaries of seed
examples, $`M_{G}`$ contextualizes the synthesized keywords into an
executable instruction $`x^{\prime}`$. Last, $`M_{G}`$ produces response
$`y^{\prime}`$ that appropriately addresses the generated instruction
$`x^{\prime}`$.

### 3.3 Data Reviewer

To ensure equitable data evaluation and mitigate individual model
biases, the Reviewer module performs a rigorous multi-agent quality
assessment through coordinated evaluation protocols. We randomly select
$`N_{R}`$ reviewers from $`\mathcal{M}\setminus{M_{G}}`$ to form the
review committee $`R=\{M_{R_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{N_{R}}`$.

The review process includes two stages: instruction evaluation and
response evaluation. During the instruction evaluation phase, each
Reviewer independently verifies instruction $`x^{\prime}`$ against three
binary criteria: “Reasonableness, Completeness, and Clarity”. Immediate
rejection occurs if any Reviewer $`M_{R_{i}}`$ flags any criterion
failure. Approved instructions then advance to the response evaluation
stage, where each Reviewer conducts a granular analysis of the generated
response $`y^{\prime}`$ from six dimensional metrics: “Correctness,
Clarity, Completeness, Relevance, Coherence, and Ethicality”. Then each
Reviewer quantitatively assesses these dimensions by assigning integer
scores from 0 to 10 and the averaged score serves as the final score.
Additionally, each Reviewer provides detailed textual feedback that
delineates both the strengths and weaknesses of the generated response.

In the end, the committee $`R`$ aggregates assessments through
calculating the mean composite score $`\mu_{R}`$ and assessing consensus
reliability through standard deviation $`\sigma_{R}`$. After all, the
committee $`R`$ makes the final decision: (a) Rejection: If
$`\mu_{R}<\tau`$. (b) Acceptance: If $`\mu_{R}\geq\tau`$ with
$`\sigma_{R}\leq\delta`$. (c). Adjudication: If $`\mu_{R}\geq\tau`$ but
$`\sigma_{R}>\delta`$, where $`\tau`$ and $`\delta`$ are predefined
thresholds.

### 3.4 Data Adjudicator

Adjudicator is designed for reassessing the disputed samples. For each
disputed sample, we randomly select an Adjudicator $`M_{A}`$ from
$`\mathcal{M}\setminus({M_{G}}\cup R)`$ to perform consensus-driven
arbitration. For each disputed sample, based on consolidating Reviewers’
feedback, $`M_{A}`$ conducts a comprehensive reassessment using the same
evaluation criteria as the Reviewers and gets the final composite score
$`s_{A}`$. Only samples with $`s_{A}\geq\tau`$ proceed to the subsequent
post-processing module.

### 3.5 Post-Processing Module

The post-processing module ensures syntactic consistency and enhances
diversity for final dataset integration. First, we generate embeddings
for all data using the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 encoder [Reimers and Gurevych
(2019)](#bib.bib33). Data are processed based on their review score
$`\mu_{R}`$ in descending order. Each sample, along with its embedding,
undergoes semantic redundancy verification against the target data pool:
if the maximum cosine similarity with any item in the pool is below a
specified similarity threshold, the candidate is added to the pool.
Otherwise, it is rejected to prevent semantic duplication. The
deduplicated data then undergoes metadata enrichment through random LLM
$`M_{P}\in\mathcal{M}`$ to generate contextual summary $`s^{\prime}`$,
supplemented with the keywords from which it was derived, ensuring
format consistency with the existing data. This two-stage
filtration—embedding-based semantic deduplication followed by LLM
summarization—ensures both conceptual diversity and structural
compatibility for subsequent data synthesis workflows.

## 4 Experiment

### 4.1 Settings

#### GRA Data Generation.

Our framework operates on three established instruction-tuning datasets:
Alpaca [Taori et al. (2023)](#bib.bib38), WizardLM [Xu et al.
(2024a)](#bib.bib41), and the recent Condor [Cao et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib4), which serve as seed datasets for data synthesis. As
for the small LLMs, we use five diverse and representative LLMs within
7B-8B parameters: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [Dubey et al.
(2024b)](#bib.bib12), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [Yang et al.
(2024b)](#bib.bib45), InternLM3-8B-Instruct [Cai et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib3), Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 [Jiang et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib19), and Tulu-3-8B [Lambert et al. (2024)](#bib.bib22).
The synthesis process runs for five iterations, and each iteration
produces approx $`10`$K high-quality samples per round ($`51`$K in
total) using vLLM [Kwon et al. (2023)](#bib.bib21) toolkit. We set the
minimum score threshold $`\tau=8`$ and the maximum standard deviation
$`\delta=1.5`$ at review stage. For deduplication, the maximum cosine
similarity is set to $`0.9`$. More detailed generation settings are
shown in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Generation ‣ A Strategic Coordination Framework of Small LLMs Matches Large LLMs in Data Synthesis").

#### Training.

After data synthesis, we conduct full parameter Supervised Fine-Tuning
(SFT) on two well-known base models for verification:
Llama-3.1-8B-Base [Dubey et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib12) and
Qwen2.5-7B-Base [Yang et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib45). The experiments
utilize the Llama-Factory [Zheng et al. (2024a)](#bib.bib49) toolkit. We
run five iterations, each accumulating synthetic data from Rnd$`1`$ to
Rnd$`5`$, representing data from the first round up to all five rounds.
In the main experiment, we report the iteration with the best average
performance. Detailed training settings are provided in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Training ‣ A Strategic Coordination Framework of Small LLMs Matches Large LLMs in Data Synthesis").

#### Evaluation.

For evaluation, following [Xu et al. (2024a)](#bib.bib41); [Cao et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib4), we select multiple benchmarks on various
domains-mathematics, coding, reasoning, and general-to demonstrate the
effectiveness of our GRA framework, which include GSM8K, MATH,
HumanEval, MBPP, HellaSwag, ARC-C, GPQA, IFEval, BBH and MMLU. We use
the opencompass [Contributors (2023b)](#bib.bib10) toolkit for a fair
evaluation. More detailed evaluation settings are shown in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Evaluation ‣ A Strategic Coordination Framework of Small LLMs Matches Large LLMs in Data Synthesis").

### 4.2 Main Results

The main results are presented in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Evaluation. ‣ 4.1 Settings ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ A Strategic Coordination Framework of Small LLMs Matches Large LLMs in Data Synthesis"),
where we compare GRA against vanilla seed datasets and also single large
LLM (Qwen2.5-32B/72B-Instruct) distillation. From the table, we can draw
following observations:

#### Superiority Over Vanilla Seed Data.

The GRA method achieves significant improvements over vanilla seed data,
with average performance gains of $`6.18`$% (Llama-3.1-8B) and
$`11.81`$% (Qwen-2.5-7B) across all benchmarks. These results
demonstrate the effectiveness of GRA. We attribute this success to GRA’s
ability to enhance data diversity and quality through iterative data
synthesis. Further analysis is provided in
Section [5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 Data Quality ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ A Strategic Coordination Framework of Small LLMs Matches Large LLMs in Data Synthesis").

#### Competitive Against Large LLM Distillation.

GRA’s collaborative small LLM framework demonstrates parity with or
superiority to single large LLM distillation. Notably, comparing to
Qwen-2.5-72B-Instruct distilled data, it narrows the performance gap to
$`0.59`$% for Llama-3.1-8B while surpassing by $`8.83`$% for Qwen-2.5-7B
on average. This validates the viability of cost-effective multi-agent
synthesis as a scalable alternative to resource-intensive large-model
distillation.

#### Base Model Dependency.

Performance varies substantially with base model capability: Qwen-based
implementations consistently outperform Llama counterparts by  9% under
identical data conditions. We attribute this discrepancy to Qwen’s
strong base model ability, as demonstrated by many recent models [Yang
et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib45), which likely enhance its ability to
leverage synthesized data.

#### Diminishing Returns in Teacher Scaling.

Despite doubling parameter counts
(Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct$`\to`$Qwen-2.5-72B-Instruct), teacher model
scaling yields marginal quality gains. This suggests a potential
saturation point in knowledge transfer efficiency for standard
distillation methods, emphasizing the need for more advanced
distillation protocols rather than naive distillation from larger
models. These insights collectively highlight GRA’s practical value for
efficient, high-quality data generation while delineating fundamental
boundaries in LLM knowledge transfer.

### 4.3 Ablation

#### Performance along Data Iteration.

To investigate the impact of iterative data synthesis rounds on model
performance, we conduct five sequential iterations of data generation
using GRA, with approx $`10`$K synthetic samples produced per iteration.
We trained models incrementally on cumulative datasets: $`10`$K ($`1`$st
iteration), $`20`$K (1st–2nd), $`30`$K ($`1`$st–$`3`$rd), $`40`$K
($`1`$st–4th), and $`50`$K ($`1`$st–$`5`$th). Results are illustrated in
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Performance along Data Iteration. ‣ 4.3 Ablation ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ A Strategic Coordination Framework of Small LLMs Matches Large LLMs in Data Synthesis").
Experiments across three distinct seed datasets consistently demonstrate
a positive correlation between iteration count and model performance.
Besides, we observe that performance gains are rapid in early
iterations, but gradually plateaued in later iterations, suggesting
diminishing yet meaningful returns. This trend aligns with the
hypothesis that initial cycles resolve critical data scarcity, whereas
subsequent rounds exhaust exploitable synthetic data diversity.

Figure 3: Performance along data iterations with Qwen-2.5-7B-Base model.

#### Effect of GRA Data Reviewer.

We conduct ablation experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of GRA’s
multi-model review mechanism by comparing against three baselines: no
Reviewer, Llama3.1-8B-Instruct Reviewer. As shown in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Effect of GRA Data Reviewer. ‣ 4.3 Ablation ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ A Strategic Coordination Framework of Small LLMs Matches Large LLMs in Data Synthesis"),
GRA outperforms all baselines, confirming the necessity of collaborative
curation. Notably, single-model reviews show negligible gains over no
review, implying either (a) limited quality-assessment capacity in small
LLMs or (b) data quality from GRA’s generation phase being sufficiently
robust for standalone use. These results validate that GRA’s multi-agent
framework uniquely synthesizes complementary curation strengths,
avoiding the pitfalls of isolated or capacity-constrained reviewers.
Comparisons wiht large LLM reviwer are shown in
Section [5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 Data Quality ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ A Strategic Coordination Framework of Small LLMs Matches Large LLMs in Data Synthesis").

Figure 4: comparison across different setting of reviewer and
adjudicator, with alpaca as seed dataset and Llama-3.1-8B as base model.

#### Effect of GRA Data Adjudicator.

To validate the necessity of the Adjudicator module in GRA, we conducted
ablation experiments without the Adjudicator, where conflicting reviews
were resolved via majority voting. Using Llama-3.1-8B as the base model
and Alpaca as the seed dataset, the Adjudicator-enhanced version
achieved a 0.73% improvement in synthetic data quality (measured by
human-aligned correctness scores), demonstrating its effectiveness, as
shown in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Effect of GRA Data Reviewer. ‣ 4.3 Ablation ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ A Strategic Coordination Framework of Small LLMs Matches Large LLMs in Data Synthesis").

## 5 Analysis

### 5.1 Effect of Small LLMs’ Role

We are interested in the specific role played in the GRA framework,
therefore we conduct experiments of three role assignment strategies for
GRA pipeline with Qwen-2.5-7B-Base as the training model: (1)
Single-Model: all roles assigned to a single LLM (Llama3.1-8B-Instruct);
(2) Fixed-assignment strategy: five distinct LLMs assigned to roles in
fixed permutations; (3) Our GRA setting with random roles. The results
are as follows: when we simply use one model to play all roles (Setting
1), the average accuracy is 52.07, while Setting 2, which assigns fixed
roles to five dedicated models, results in a lower accuracy of 48.59.
Lastly, our GRA based training achieves 59.52 accuracy. Lastly, our GRA
based training achieves 59.52 accuracy. From the above results, we can
find that the advantages of our randomized role assignment in our GRA is
clear and significant, compared to both other settings. Besides,
interestingly, fixed assignments of different models performs worse than
single role model, which means that self-evolve is better than fixed
role assignment among different models, further demonstrating that
multi-agent corporation is curial.

### 5.2 Inconsistent Data Analysis

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Case 1: A case analysis of inconsistent data.

We show a
Case [1](#S5.T1 "Case 1 ‣ 5.2 Inconsistent Data Analysis ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ A Strategic Coordination Framework of Small LLMs Matches Large LLMs in Data Synthesis")
to further illustrate the effectiveness of Adjudicator. For a wrong math
problem, two of three reviewers incorrectly assigned high scores, while
one correctly flagged the error. Although the average score ($`8/10`$)
initially met the retention threshold, the high score variance
($`2.48`$) triggered adjudication. The Adjudicator synthesized all
reviews and evaluation criteria, overriding the majority’s misjudgment
to assign a low score ($`4.5/10`$), thereby filtering out the flawed
data. This highlights how the Adjudicator mitigates limitations of
simple voting or averaging by dynamically reconciling disagreements and
enforcing rigorous quality standards.

### 5.3 Data Diversity

To assess the diversity of synthesized data, we compare three sources:
GRA-generated data, data distilled from a single large LLM, and the
vanilla seed dataset. We visualize the instruction embeddings with
t-SNE [Van der Maaten and Hinton (2008)](#bib.bib39).

#### Diversity Analysis.

As shown in
Figure [6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 5.2 Inconsistent Data Analysis ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ A Strategic Coordination Framework of Small LLMs Matches Large LLMs in Data Synthesis").
GRA-generated data exhibits a broader distribution than the vanilla seed
dataset, particularly covering underrepresented regions in the seed
data’s embedding space. This suggests that GRA complementing the seed
dataset by expanding its coverage. Besides,
Figure [6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 5.2 Inconsistent Data Analysis ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ A Strategic Coordination Framework of Small LLMs Matches Large LLMs in Data Synthesis")
reveals that GRA surpasses the single large LLM in distribution
diversity, implying that collaborative small LLMs can mitigate the
inherent limits and biases of single model. Notably, while the seed
dataset demonstrates comparable instruction diversity, its inferior
performance in main experiments-Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Evaluation. ‣ 4.1 Settings ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ A Strategic Coordination Framework of Small LLMs Matches Large LLMs in Data Synthesis")
highlights critical deficiencies in response quality rather than
instruction coverage.

#### Seed Data Enhancement via GRA.

We further applied GRA’s generator to rewrite responses in the vanilla
seed dataset, followed by curation using GRA’s reviewer and adjudicator.
As shown in Table
[2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Seed Data Enhancement via GRA. ‣ 5.3 Data Diversity ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ A Strategic Coordination Framework of Small LLMs Matches Large LLMs in Data Synthesis"),
the refined dataset achieves performance parity with GRA-generated data.
Moreover, combining GRA-synthesized data with enhanced seed data yields
synergistic effects, outperforming either dataset alone in certain
settings. This underscores GRA’s dual utility: (a) generating novel
high-quality data and (b) upgrading existing data through systematic
rewriting and quality control.

### 5.4 Data Quality

To evaluate the data quality, we utilize Qwen-2.5-72B-Instruct to assess
the synthetic data and compare its score with our Reviewers’ score. From
Figure [7](#S5.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 5.4 Data Quality ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ A Strategic Coordination Framework of Small LLMs Matches Large LLMs in Data Synthesis"),
we find that the GRA method exhibits finer granularity and a more
balanced scoring distribution compared to the coarser-grained scores
from the large LLM, indicating its ability to capture nuanced quality
variations. Second, over $`87.3`$% of GRA-curated data (scores $`>8`$)
align with high scores from the large LLM, while $`12.7`$% receive lower
scores ($`\leq 8`$) from the latter. Notably, the large LLM assigns even
higher scores to a larger subset of data, further validating the
reliability of GRA in generating high-quality data. These results
suggest that GRA enhances scoring resolution without compromising
assessment consistency with large LLMs.

Figure 7: Data quality score comparison between GRA and single Large
LLMs—Qwen-2.5-72B-Instruct.

### 5.5 Data Difficulty

To evaluate the complexity and knowledge density of synthesized data, we
compute the Instruction-Following Difficulty (IFD) score [Li et al.
(2024b)](#bib.bib25) for the three datasets. From the results depicted
in
Figure [8](#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 5.5 Data Difficulty ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ A Strategic Coordination Framework of Small LLMs Matches Large LLMs in Data Synthesis"),
two key observations emerge: First, GRA-generated data achieves a
significantly higher IFD than the seed dataset ($`+14.58`$%), indicating
its enhanced difficulty and richer knowledge coverage. This aligns with
empirical training results, where models trained on GRA data exhibit
superior performance. Second, despite using smaller LLMs, GRA attains
comparable difficulty to the Qwen-72B-distilled data ($`75.82`$% v.s.
$`75.49`$%). This suggests that collaborative small LLMs in GRA mitigate
individual capability limitations, effectively emulating large LLMs in
generating challenging examples. These results validate GRA’s ability to
synthesize high-quality, difficulty-controllable data without relying on
large LLMs, addressing both scalability and performance trade-offs in
data synthesis pipelines.

Figure 8: The IFD score comparison between the data generated by GRA,
the vanilla seed dataset WizardLM, and single large LLM
(Qwen-2.5-72B-Instruct) distilled data.

## 6 Conclusion

In this paper, we introduce GRA (Generator-Reviewer-Adjudicator), a
novel framework that leverages the collaborative capabilities of
multiple small LLMs to achieve data synthesis quality comparable to that
of single monolithic LLMs. Our approach addresses the significant
computational and environmental concerns associated with large LLMs
while mitigating the biases inherent in their centralized architectures.
The experimental results across diverse benchmarks validate the efficacy
of GRA. GRA underscores the potential of role specialization in
enhancing data synthesis quality, challenging the prevailing notion that
larger models are inherently superior for such tasks, paving the way for
more sustainable and equitable data synthesis.

## Limitations

Despite the promising performance of the GRA framework, several aspects
warrant further exploration. Current role allocation mechanism—based on
randomized assignment—may yield suboptimal collaboration patterns. This
stochastic approach lacks explicit optimization for task-specific
synergies, suggesting the need for intelligent role configuration
strategies (e.g., performance-aware dynamic allocation or metric-driven
reinforcement learning) to systematically maximize agent
complementarity. Furthermore, while GRA is primarily designed for
textual reasoning tasks, extending its paradigm to multimodal scenarios
presents a compelling direction.

## Appendix A Generation

When generating data, we deployed models using VLLM and
LMDeploy [Contributors (2023a)](#bib.bib9) on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. For
setting the model generation parameters, we used the default settings of
the deployment tools, except for temperature=0.2, top_p=0.9,
max_token=4096. The number of examples used in few-shot ranges from
$`2`$ to $`4`$. We set the minimum score threshold $`\tau=8`$ and the
maximum standard deviation $`\delta=1.5`$ at review stage. For
deduplication, the maximum cosine similarity is set to $`0.9`$. Here we
provide detailed criteria for data domain classification:

- •
  Coding: Involves understanding, generating, debugging, and fixing
  code.
- •
  Math: Entails performing mathematical operations, applying formulas,
  and solving problems.
- •
  QA: Focuses on providing specialized and accurate answers to questions
  within a specific domain or field.
- •
  Language: Involves accurately understanding and analyzing text,
  performing tasks such as translation, summarization, and
  classification.
- •
  Role Play: Engages in simulated conversations or behaviors by assuming
  different roles to explore various perspectives or scenarios.
- •
  Reasoning: Involves complex causal reasoning and logical judgment,
  solving multi-level problems through inference and analysis.
- •
  Creation: Emphasizes originality and creativity, creating content
  according to requirements and adapting to different styles and themes.

Before initiating the GRA data synthesis, we employed all available LLMs
to extract keywords and summaries from the seed dataset using a
randomized rotation approach.

## Appendix B Training

We employ LLaMA-Factory ([Zheng et al., 2024a](#bib.bib49)) for model
fine-tuning. All models, including our reproduced baselines, are
fine-tuned over 1 epochs with a batch size of 256 using 8 NVIDIA A100
GPUs. The peak learning rate is set to 5e-6, featuring a linear warm-up
during the initial 3% of training steps, followed by a cosine decay. The
maximum sequence length is configured to 4096.

## Appendix C Evaluation

We compare GRA with baselines on the following 10 benchmarks:

- •
  The GSM8K dataset ([Cobbe et al., 2021](#bib.bib8)) contains 8,500
  grade school-level math word problems.focus on real-world scenarios,
  testing a model’s ability to parse natural language, extract relevant
  information, and perform accurate calculations.
- •
  The MATH dataset ([Hendrycks et al., 2021](#bib.bib17)) evaluates
  mathematical reasoning with problems spanning arithmetic, algebra,
  calculus, and geometry, and 5 levels of difficulty.
- •
  The HumanEval dataset ([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib6)) is designed to
  evaluate the functional correctness of code generation models. It
  consists of 164 hand-written programming problems, each requiring the
  generation of a Python function to solve a specific task. The dataset
  assesses the ability of models to produce syntactically correct and
  logically accurate code.
- •
  The MBPP dataset ([Austin et al., 2021](#bib.bib2)) contains around
  1,000 Python programming tasks, focusing on fundamental programming
  concepts. It is split into training and test sets, with tasks ranging
  from simple operations to more complex algorithmic challenges, making
  it suitable for evaluating code generation and understanding.
- •
  The Hellaswag dataset ([Zellers et al., 2019](#bib.bib47)) is a
  commonsense reasoning benchmark that includes 70,000 multiple-choice
  questions derived from everyday scenarios. It tests a model’s ability
  to predict the most plausible continuation of a given context,
  emphasizing natural language understanding and reasoning.
- •
  The ARC-C dataset ([Clark et al., 2018](#bib.bib7)) is a collection of
  science exam questions designed to evaluate advanced reasoning
  capabilities. It includes 2,590 questions across various science
  topics, requiring multi-step reasoning and knowledge application to
  solve.
- •
  The GPQA datase ([Rein et al., 2023](#bib.bib34))t is a high-quality
  benchmark for evaluating general knowledge and reasoning. It consists
  of diverse questions spanning multiple domains, including science,
  history, and culture, designed to test the breadth and depth of a
  model’s understanding.
- •
  The IFEval dataset ([Zhou et al., 2023](#bib.bib51)) focuses on
  evaluating instruction-following capabilities in language models. It
  includes a variety of tasks that require models to follow complex
  instructions accurately, testing their ability to understand and
  execute multi-step directives.
- •
  The MMLU dataset ([Hendrycks et al., 2020](#bib.bib16)) is a
  comprehensive benchmark covering 57 tasks across diverse domains,
  including humanities, STEM, and social sciences. It evaluates a
  model’s ability to perform well across a wide range of subjects and
  tasks.
- •
  The BBH dataset ([Suzgun et al., 2022](#bib.bib37)) is a subset of the
  Big-Bench benchmark, consisting of 23 challenging tasks that are
  particularly difficult for language models. These tasks require
  advanced reasoning, knowledge, and problem-solving skills, making them
  a robust test of model capabilities.

  In our testing, we employ the default metrics of
  OpenCompass ([Contributors, 2023b](#bib.bib10)) corresponding to each
  benchmark.
